claim: The CPTAC dataset comprises about 700 tumor samples derived from seven tumor types: colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), breast cancer (BRCA), ovarian cancer (OV), clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC), HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD).
source: Here, we analyzed CPTAC data comprising about 700 tumor samples derived from seven tumor types: colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), breast cancer (BRCA), ovarian cancer (OV), clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC), HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the composition of the CPTAC dataset analyzed.

claim: The CPTAC dataset contains information at the DNA level by whole-genome sequencing (WGS) or whole-exome sequencing (WES), RNA level by RNAseq and protein level by TMT mass spectrometry for 7–12K genes.
source: The dataset contains information at the DNA level by whole-genome sequencing (WGS) or whole-exome sequencing (WES), RNA level by RNAseq and protein level by TMT mass spectrometry for 7–12K genes (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the types of data and number of genes in the CPTAC dataset.

claim: RNA levels change proportionally to the DNA levels in aneuploid cells (i.e., there is no RNA-level compensation) while the protein levels do not (i.e., there is protein-level compensation).
source: Work done in model organisms and isogenic human cells suggests that RNA levels change proportionally to the DNA levels in aneuploid cells (i.e., there is no RNA-level compensation) while the protein levels do not (i.e., there is protein-level compensation) (Oromendia et al., 2012; Stingele et al., 2012; Torres et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work in model organisms and isogenic human cells.

claim: In the pan-cancer analysis, there was significant protein-level compensation (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.001) and no significant RNA-level compensation except in the high gain group.
source: In our pan-cancer analysis (Figure 1B), this was generally the case, with a significant protein-level compensation (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.001) and no significant RNA-level compensation except in the high gain group (see also below; FDR < 0.001; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results from the pan-cancer dataset shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Protein-level compensation was significant for both gains and losses, although it was stronger in the high gain group versus the deep loss group (FDR < 0.001).
source: Protein-level compensation was significant for both gains and losses, although it was stronger in the high gain group versus the deep loss group (FDR < 0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of protein-level compensation between different DNA copy number groups.

claim: LUAD did not show protein-level compensation (FDR = 1).
source: While protein-level compensation was widespread, LUAD did not show protein-level compensation (FDR = 1, Supplementary file 1C)
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of protein-level compensation in LUAD based on statistical analysis.

claim: BRCA showed reduced protein-level compensation compared to other cancer types, especially for DNA losses.
source: BRCA showed reduced protein-level compensation compared to other cancer types, especially for DNA losses (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports tissue-specific differences in protein-level compensation.

claim: COAD showed general RNA-level compensation both for gains and losses (FDR < 0.001).
source: COAD showed general RNA-level compensation both for gains and losses (FDR < 0.001, Supplementary file 1C; degree of compensation was lower for deep loss than other SCNA groups).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-level compensation in COAD based on statistical analysis.

claim: ccRCC showed RNA-level compensation for deep losses (FDR < 0.001).
source: In addition, ccRCC showed RNA-level compensation for deep losses (FDR < 0.001)
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-level compensation in ccRCC for specific DNA copy number changes.

claim: BRCA exhibited RNA-level compensation for high gains (FDR < 0.001).
source: and BRCA exhibited RNA-level compensation for high gains (FDR < 0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-level compensation in BRCA for high gains.

claim: OV showed RNA-level compensation for non-complex genes but not for complex genes in all SCNA groups.
source: Interestingly, OV showed RNA-level compensation for non-complex genes but not for complex genes in all SCNA groups (Figure 1C and D, Supplementary file 1C, see below).
evidence: The manuscript reports differential RNA-level compensation between complex and non-complex genes in OV.

claim: Protein complex genes had a stronger protein-level compensation compared to non-complex genes (Figure 1B, FDR < 0.001).
source: In general, we found that protein complex genes had a stronger protein-level compensation compared to non-complex genes (Figure 1B, FDR < 0.001, Supplementary file 1D), consistent with previous studies examining the effect of chromosome gains (Oromendia et al., 2012; Stingele et al., 2012; Torres et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis comparing protein-level compensation between complex and non-complex genes, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Protein complex genes showed stronger protein-level compensation not only for gains, but also for losses (Figure 1B, FDR < 0.001).
source: Importantly, this was true not only for gains, but also for losses (Figure 1B, FDR < 0.001, Supplementary file 1D)
evidence: The manuscript reports that the difference in protein-level compensation between complex and non-complex genes applies to both gains and losses.

claim: Protein complex genes showed stronger protein-level compensation across tumor types (Figure 1C, FDR < 0.001).
source: and across tumor types (Figure 1C, FDR < 0.001, Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports that the difference in protein-level compensation between complex and non-complex genes is consistent across different tumor types.

claim: At the RNA level, protein complex genes showed less RNA-level compensation compared to non-complex genes for high DNA gain (Figure 1B, FDR < 0.001).
source: Interestingly, at the RNA level, the opposite was true: protein complex genes showed less RNA-level compensation compared to non-complex genes for high DNA gain, the only group showing significant compensation in the pan-cancer analysis (Figure 1B, FDR < 0.001, Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports differential RNA-level compensation between complex and non-complex genes.

claim: In the majority of tumor types showing significant RNA-level compensation, complex genes showed less RNA-level compensation compared to non-complex genes (high gain group of BRCA and all groups of OV, Figure 1C, FDR < 0.001).
source: As mentioned above, for the individual tumor types, only certain cancers showed significant RNA-level compensation; in the majority of those cases, complex genes showed less RNA-level compensation compared to non-complex genes (high gain group of BRCA and all groups of OV, Figure 1C, FDR < 0.001, Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports tissue-specific patterns of differential RNA-level compensation.

claim: OV showed significant RNA-level compensation for non-complex genes but not for complex genes across all DNA groups (Figure 1C, FDR < 0.001).
source: For example, OV showed significant RNA-level compensation for non-complex genes but not for complex genes across all DNA groups (Figure 1C, FDR < 0.001, Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific findings for OV regarding differential RNA-level compensation.

claim: Both ribosomal and non-ribosomal complex genes showed significant compensation at the protein level for both gains and losses.
source: Both ribosomal and non-ribosomal complex genes showed significant compensation at the protein level for both gains and losses, indicating that our results are not dependent on ribosomal genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis excluding ribosomal genes to validate the findings.

claim: The protein-level compensation of ribosomal genes was so strong that the median protein log2FC remained almost unchanged for high gains and deep losses.
source: Notably, the protein-level compensation of ribosomal genes was so strong that the median protein log2FC remained almost unchanged for high gains and deep losses; this was not the case for the RNA level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports the degree of protein-level compensation for ribosomal genes.

claim: TMT-based proteome quantifications suffer from the issue of ratio compression and may underestimate the actual change.
source: TMT-based proteome quantifications, widely adopted in CPTAC database, suffer from the issue of ratio compression and may underestimate the actual change (Savitski et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study describing a technical limitation of TMT mass spectrometry.

claim: Previous studies using other techniques such as SILAC or MS3-based proteomics found widespread protein compensation for complex genes after DNA gain in yeast and pairs of isogenic diploid and aneuploid cell lines.
source: Nevertheless, previous studies using other techniques such as stable isotope labeling with amino acids in cell culture (SILAC) or MS3-based proteomics found widespread protein compensation for complex genes after DNA gain in yeast and pairs of isogenic diploid and aneuploid cell lines, consistent with our observations (Dephoure et al., 2014; Hwang et al., 2021; Stingele et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies using alternative methods that support the findings.

claim: Label-free proteomics analysis of TCGA COAD samples showed significant compensation at the protein level, which is higher for complex genes than non-complex genes.
source: To further exclude the impact of ratio compression on our results, we performed the analysis shown in Figure 1 on The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA; Weinstein et al., 2013) COAD samples for which label-free proteomics data is available (Zhang et al., 2014). Consistent with TMT-based proteomics, significant compensation at the protein level was found, which is higher for complex genes than non-complex genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation using an alternative proteomics method.

claim: For COAD, RNA-level compensation was shown in all groups of DNA change and was stronger for non-complex genes (deep loss and high gain, FDR < 0.005).
source: As we observed before, for COAD (Figure 1C), RNA-level compensation was shown in all groups of DNA change and was stronger for non-complex genes (deep loss and high gain, FDR < 0.005, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-level compensation patterns in COAD using label-free proteomics data.

claim: The limitations imposed by the TMT quantification do not affect the results of the analyses.
source: These additional observations indicate that the limitations imposed by the TMT quantification do not affect the results of our analyses.
evidence: The manuscript concludes that technical limitations do not impact the findings based on validation experiments.

claim: Genome doubling is common in cancer and may affect the calculation of relative changes of DNA, RNA, or protein.
source: Another possible confounder is genome doubling, which is common in cancer and may affect the calculation of relative changes of DNA, RNA, or protein.
evidence: The manuscript identifies genome doubling as a potential confounding factor based on established knowledge.

claim: Analysis of TCGA samples excluding genome doubling showed widespread protein compensation for complex genes and RNA compensation for non-complex genes, consistent with the main analysis.
source: To exclude the interference of genome doubling, we analyzed the proteomics data for TCGA samples (Mertins et al., 2016; the Zhang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016), for which this information is available. Samples inferred by ABSOLUTE (Carter et al., 2012) to have undergone genome doubling, were removed from the analysis. Consistent with Figure 1C, widespread protein compensation was observed for complex genes, and RNA compensation was observed for non-complex genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 1H).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation analysis excluding samples with genome doubling.

claim: The presence of genome doubling in a fraction of the samples does not affect the results of the analyses.
source: Therefore, these data indicate that the presence of genome doubling in a fraction of the samples does not affect the results of our analyses.
evidence: The manuscript concludes that genome doubling does not confound the findings based on validation experiments.

claim: CCLE analysis showed general protein-level compensation and negligible RNA-level compensation except in the deep loss group at the pan-cancer level (FDR < 0.001).
source: To validate the findings observed from primary tumors, we performed the same analysis on cancer cell lines using the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) (Barretina et al., 2012; Nusinow et al., 2020), which showed general protein-level compensation and negligible RNA-level compensation except in the deep loss group at the pan-cancer level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, FDR < 0.001, Supplementary file 1I).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation of findings using cancer cell line data.

claim: In CCLE, protein complex genes had stronger protein-level compensation than non-complex genes similar to primary tumors (FDR < 0.001).
source: Protein complex genes had stronger protein-level compensation than non-complex genes similar to primary tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, FDR < 0.001, Supplementary file 1J).
evidence: The manuscript reports that findings in primary tumors are replicated in cancer cell lines.

claim: hTERT-immortalized TP53-KO hCEC were treated with reversine to induce random chromosome missegregation and subsequent aneuploidy.
source: We treated hTERT-immortalized TP53-KO (non-tumorigenic) hCEC (Ly et al., 2011; Sack et al., 2018) with reversine, an MPS1 inhibitor that inhibits correct chromosome attachment and spindle checkpoint, to induce random chromosome missegregation and subsequent aneuploidy (Santaguida et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method used to generate aneuploid cell lines.

claim: hCEC showed RNA-level compensation as COAD did (FDR < 0.001).
source: Interestingly, in addition to the widespread protein-level compensation, hCEC also showed RNA-level compensation as COAD did (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, FDR < 0.001, Supplementary file 1L).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-level compensation in isogenic aneuploid cell lines.

claim: In hCEC, complex genes had stronger protein-level compensation for the DNA gain and deep loss groups but weaker RNA-level compensation for the DNA loss group (FDR = 0.013).
source: Similar to COAD primary tumors, in hCEC complex genes had stronger protein-level compensation for the DNA gain and deep loss groups but weaker RNA-level compensation for the DNA loss group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, FDR = 0.013, Supplementary file 1M).
evidence: The manuscript reports differential compensation patterns between complex and non-complex genes in hCEC.

claim: While protein-level compensation is widespread and RNA-level compensation is virtually absent in the pan-cancer analysis, there is significant tissue specificity especially in the presence and degree of RNA-level compensation.
source: Overall, these data suggest that while protein-level compensation is widespread and RNA-level compensation is virtually absent in our pan-cancer analysis, there is significant tissue specificity especially in the presence and degree of RNA-level compensation.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings regarding tissue-specific patterns of compensation.

claim: Protein complex genes generally showed stronger protein-level compensation and weaker RNA-level compensation compared to non-complex genes.
source: Furthermore, protein complex genes generally showed stronger protein-level compensation and weaker RNA-level compensation compared to non-complex genes.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the general finding regarding differences between complex and non-complex genes.

claim: If the correlation between RNA and protein is very high, the protein abundance is mainly determined by the RNA amount with minimal protein-level regulation.
source: In other words, if the correlation between RNA and protein is very high, we can infer that the protein abundance is mainly determined by the RNA amount with minimal protein-level regulation.
evidence: The manuscript explains the logic for inferring protein-level regulation from RNA-protein correlation.

claim: If the correlation between RNA and protein is low, there is a strong level of protein-level regulation.
source: On the other hand, if the correlation between RNA and protein is low, we assume a strong level of protein-level regulation.
evidence: The manuscript explains the logic for inferring protein-level regulation from RNA-protein correlation.

claim: A similar logic can be used to infer the RNA-level regulation based on the DNA–RNA correlation.
source: A similar logic can be used to infer the RNA-level regulation based on the DNA–RNA correlation.
evidence: The manuscript explains the logic for inferring RNA-level regulation from DNA-RNA correlation.

claim: The median of the RNA–protein correlations was significantly lower for protein complex genes than for non-complex genes (FDR < 0.001).
source: As expected, we found that the median of the RNA–protein correlations was significantly lower for protein complex genes than for non-complex genes (FDR < 0.001), indicating that protein complex genes tend to have stronger protein-level regulation compared to non-complex genes (Stingele et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of RNA-protein correlations between complex and non-complex genes, supported by citation.

claim: The median of the DNA–RNA correlations was significantly higher for protein complex genes than for non-complex genes (FDR < 0.001).
source: Strikingly, the opposite was true for RNA-level regulation, where the median of the DNA–RNA correlations was significantly higher for protein complex genes than for non-complex genes (FDR < 0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of DNA-RNA correlations between complex and non-complex genes.

claim: The difference in DNA-RNA correlations between complex and non-complex genes was not due to the difference in the RNA abundance.
source: In addition, it was not due to the difference in the RNA abundance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; analysis repeated with the exclusion of genes of low RNA abundance)
evidence: The manuscript reports control analysis excluding low-abundance genes.

claim: The difference in DNA-RNA correlations between complex and non-complex genes was not due to difference in the variance of DNA alterations between protein complex and non-complex genes.
source: or difference in the variance of DNA alterations between protein complex and non-complex genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; ANOVA across DNA values)
evidence: The manuscript reports control analysis examining DNA variance.

claim: The difference in DNA-RNA correlations between complex and non-complex genes was not due to the fact that ribosomal complex genes make up the majority of complex genes.
source: or to the fact that ribosomal complex genes make up the majority of complex genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; analysis repeated with the exclusion of ribosomal genes).
evidence: The manuscript reports control analysis excluding ribosomal genes.

claim: Protein complex genes are likely to have weaker RNA-level regulation compared to non-complex genes.
source: This result indicates that protein complex genes are likely to have weaker RNA-level regulation compared to non-complex genes.
evidence: The manuscript infers weaker RNA-level regulation for complex genes based on DNA-RNA correlation analysis.

claim: For protein complex genes, the median DNA–RNA correlation is 0.44 and the median RNA–protein correlation is 0.36 in the pan-cancer analysis.
source: We also note that in terms of absolute correlation values (Spearman's correlation), protein complex genes have lower RNA–protein correlations compared to DNA–RNA correlation values (median DNA–RNA correlation: 0.44; median RNA–protein correlation: 0.36 for protein complex genes, pan-cancer analysis)
evidence: The manuscript reports specific correlation values for protein complex genes.

claim: For non-complex genes, the median DNA–RNA correlation is 0.31 and the median RNA–protein correlation is 0.42 in the pan-cancer analysis.
source: while it is the opposite for non-complex genes (median DNA–RNA correlation: 0.31; median RNA–RNA–protein correlation: 0.42 for non-complex genes, pan-cancer analysis, Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific correlation values for non-complex genes.

claim: The finding that DNA–RNA correlations were higher and RNA–protein correlations were lower for protein complex genes than for non-complex genes was recapitulated across all seven tumor types individually (FDR < 0.001).
source: We next extended these analyses to the seven tumor types individually and observed that this result found in the pan-cancer analysis was recapitulated across all of them (FDR < 0.001, Figure 2D, Supplementary file 2B–H).
evidence: The manuscript reports that findings are consistent across individual tumor types.

claim: The finding regarding differential DNA-RNA and RNA-protein correlations between complex and non-complex genes was confirmed using CCLE and NCI-60 datasets.
source: Furthermore, this finding was confirmed using other proteogenomic datasets of cancer cell lines such as CCLE and NCI-60 (Alley et al., 1988; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation using additional cancer cell line datasets.

claim: DNA–RNA correlations were significantly higher for protein complex genes than for non-complex genes in the TCGA dataset containing additional tumor types.
source: For the DNA–RNA correlation analysis, we also used the TCGA dataset containing additional tumor types with DNA and RNA information and confirmed that DNA–RNA correlations were significantly higher for protein complex genes than for non-complex genes (Supplementary file 2I).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation using TCGA dataset.

claim: In isogenic untransformed hCEC with different aneuploid patterns, the DNA–RNA correlation was significantly higher and the RNA–protein correlation was significantly lower among protein complex genes than those among non-complex genes.
source: Using our panel of isogenic untransformed hCEC with different aneuploid patterns (Supplementary file 1H), we confirmed that the DNA–RNA correlation was significantly higher and the RNA–protein correlation was significantly lower among protein complex genes than those among non-complex (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation using isogenic non-transformed cell lines.

claim: In normal tissues, RNA–protein correlation was lower for complex genes compared to non-complex genes.
source: Finally, we interrogated a database of normal tissues that includes RNA and protein levels for the RNA–protein correlations (DNA–RNA correlations were absent as SCNAs are generally not present in normal tissues; Wang et al., 2019). Similarly, even in the normal tissues, we confirmed the lower RNA–protein correlation for complex genes compared to non-complex genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation using normal tissue data.

claim: Protein complex genes have a stronger protein-level regulation and a weaker RNA-level regulation compared to non-complex genes.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that protein complex genes have a stronger protein-level regulation and a weaker RNA-level regulation compared to non-complex genes.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding regarding differences in regulation between complex and non-complex genes.

claim: The findings in tumors or tumor cell lines are recapitulated in untransformed isogenic aneuploid cells as well as normal tissues.
source: These results also indicate that our findings in tumors or tumor cell lines are recapitulated in untransformed isogenic aneuploid cells as well as normal tissues.
evidence: The manuscript concludes that findings are generalizable based on validation in multiple systems.

claim: Some biophysical properties including protein polyampholyte score, protein polarity, and protein aggregation score had no significant association with the type of gene regulation.
source: Some of these properties, including protein polyampholyte score, protein polarity, and protein aggregation score, had no significant association with the type of gene regulation (Supplementary file 2J).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of biophysical properties and their lack of association with gene regulation.

claim: The non-exponential degradation score was predictive of strong regulation at the protein level, consistent with previous findings.
source: The non-exponential degradation score, a score representing the likelihood that a protein is degraded in a non-exponential way (McShane et al., 2016), was predictive of strong regulation at the protein level, consistent with previous findings (McShane et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports association between non-exponential degradation and protein-level regulation, supported by citation.

claim: The evolutionary conservation score (phyloP score) was associated with the RNA-level and protein-level regulation.
source: Interestingly, the evolutionary conservation score (phyloP score) (Hubisz et al., 2011) was associated with the RNA-level and protein-level regulation.
evidence: The manuscript reports association between evolutionary conservation and gene regulation.

claim: More conserved genes tended to have lower RNA–protein correlation and higher DNA–RNA correlation compared to less conserved genes (FDR < 0.001).
source: When we compared genes with high versus low conservation, we found that more conserved genes tended to have lower RNA–protein correlation and higher DNA–RNA correlation compared to less conserved genes, and thus stronger protein-level regulation and weaker RNA-level regulation (Figure 2F and G; FDR < 0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of the relationship between conservation and gene regulation.

claim: The conservation score was significantly higher for protein complex genes than non-complex genes (mean: 0.11 vs. 0.09, FDR < 0.001; variance: 0.31 vs. 0.34, p=0.004).
source: The conservation score was also significantly higher for protein complex genes than non-complex genes (Figure 2G, mean: 0.11 vs. 0.09, FDR < 0.001; variance: 0.31 vs. 0.34, p=0.004).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of conservation scores between complex and non-complex genes.

claim: Protein complex genes are more evolutionarily conserved.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that protein complex genes are more evolutionarily conserved
evidence: The manuscript concludes that protein complex genes are more conserved based on phyloP score analysis.

claim: Genes that are highly conserved tend to have a strong regulation at the protein level and vice versa.
source: and that genes that are highly conserved tend to have a strong regulation at the protein level and vice versa (see 'Discussion').
evidence: The manuscript concludes that conservation is associated with protein-level regulation.

claim: There is a significant negative association between DNA–RNA and RNA–protein correlations across genes from different CPTAC tumors (slope = −0.33, rho = −0.78, p=7.9E-07).
source: Interestingly, we found a significant negative association between these two parameters (slope = −0.33, rho = −0.78, p=7.9E-07 see 'Methods', Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing negative association between DNA-RNA and RNA-protein correlations.

claim: Genes showing a high DNA–RNA correlation tend to have a low RNA–protein correlation and vice versa.
source: In other words, genes showing a high DNA–RNA correlation tend to have a low RNA–protein correlation and vice versa.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the negative association between DNA-RNA and RNA-protein correlations.

claim: Group 1 genes (high DNA–RNA correlation and low RNA–protein correlation) were strongly enriched in mitochondrial pathways (e.g., mitochondrial translation; FDR = 4.5E-43).
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis showed that Group 1 was strongly enriched in mitochondrial pathways (Supplementary file 3B-I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; e.g., mitochondrial translation in pan-cancer; FDR = 4.5E- 43)
evidence: The manuscript reports GO enrichment analysis results for Group 1 genes.

claim: Group 1 genes were enriched in protein translation pathways (e.g., ribosome biogenesis; FDR = 3.3E-23 and cytoplasmic translation; FDR = 1.0E-07).
source: protein translation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 3B-I; e.g., ribosome biogenesis; FDR = 3.3E-23 and cytoplasmic translation in pan-cancer; FDR = 1.0E-07)
evidence: The manuscript reports GO enrichment analysis results for Group 1 genes.

claim: Group 1 genes were enriched in RNA processing pathways (e.g., RNA splicing; FDR = 4.6E-29 and non-coding-RNA metabolism; FDR = 6.0E-23).
source: and RNA processing (Supplementary file 3B-I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; e.g., RNA splicing; FDR = 4.6E-29 and non-coding-RNA metabolism; FDR = 6.0E-23).
evidence: The manuscript reports GO enrichment analysis results for Group 1 genes.

claim: Group 2 genes (low DNA–RNA correlation and high RNA–protein correlation) were enriched in cell structure pathways (e.g., actin filament organization; FDR = 9.4E-10).
source: On the other hand, Group 2 was enriched in cell structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 3B-I; e.g., actin filament organization; FDR = 9.4E-10)
evidence: The manuscript reports GO enrichment analysis results for Group 2 genes.

claim: Group 2 genes were enriched in cell adhesion pathways (e.g., substrate adhesion, FDR = 2.1E-17 and matrix adhesion, FDR = 2.2E-11).
source: cell adhesion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 3B-I; e.g., substrate adhesion, FDR = 2.1E-17 and matrix adhesion, FDR = 2.2E-11)
evidence: The manuscript reports GO enrichment analysis results for Group 2 genes.

claim: Group 2 genes were enriched in cell migration pathways (FDR = 0.044).
source: and cell migration (FDR = 0.044).
evidence: The manuscript reports GO enrichment analysis results for Group 2 genes.

claim: The pathway enrichment analysis in Groups 1 and 2 was validated using the CCLE dataset.
source: Importantly, the result of the pathway enrichment analysis in the two groups of genes (Groups 1 and 2) was validated using the CCLE dataset (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation of pathway enrichment findings using cancer cell line data.

claim: There is a strong negative correlation between the pathway-level DNA–RNA and RNA–protein correlations (rho = −0.75, p = 1.7E-07).
source: Strikingly, we found a strong negative correlation between the pathway-level DNA–RNA and RNA–protein correlations (rho = −0.75, p = 1.7E-07; Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing negative correlation at the pathway level.

claim: RNA processing and translation pathways showed a preference for high DNA–RNA and low RNA–protein correlations.
source: In agreement with our previous enrichment analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), RNA processing and translation pathways showed a preference for high DNA–RNA and low RNA–protein correlations
evidence: The manuscript reports pathway-level correlation patterns consistent with enrichment analysis.

claim: Cell adhesion and matrix-related pathways tended to have high RNA–protein and low DNA–RNA correlations.
source: while cell adhesion and matrix-related pathways tended to have high RNA–protein and low DNA–RNA correlations (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The manuscript reports pathway-level correlation patterns for cell adhesion pathways.

claim: A similar negative correlation between pathway-level DNA–RNA and RNA–protein correlations was obtained when the analysis was performed within each individual tumor type.
source: While this analysis was performed at the pan-cancer level, a similar result was obtained when we performed the analysis within each individual tumor type (Supplementary file 3K, significant negative correlation between the pathway-level DNA–RNA and RNA–protein correlations among all tumor types)
evidence: The manuscript reports that pathway-level findings are consistent across individual tumor types.

claim: The negative association among pathways reflects a general property of gene regulation independent of tissue type.
source: indicating that it reflects a general property of gen regulation independent of tissue type.
evidence: The manuscript infers that the negative association is a general property based on consistency across tumor types.

claim: The negative association between pathway-level DNA–RNA and RNA–protein correlations was confirmed based on the CCLE and NCI-60 datasets and based on isogenic hCEC data.
source: Importantly, these results were confirmed based on the CCLE and NCI-60 datasets and based on our isogenic hCEC data (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 3J).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation using multiple independent datasets.

claim: A significant negative association among pathways was maintained when calculated considering only complex genes (rho = −0.58, p = 0.00037) or non-complex genes (rho = −0.54, p = 0.00078).
source: Furthermore, a significant negative association among pathways was maintained when we calculated it considering only complex genes (rho = −0.58, p = 0.00037 ) or non-complex genes (rho = −0.54, p = 0.00078) using the CPTAC dataset (as in Figure 3B)
evidence: The manuscript reports that the negative association is not simply due to differences in complex gene composition.

claim: The negative correlation between pathway-level DNA–RNA and RNA–protein correlations was not an artifact due to different variance in the DNA values across genes.
source: Finally, we also confirmed the negative correlation was not an artifact due to different variance in the DNA values across genes, that is, by the fact that the genes in certain pathways were more likely to be gained or lost than the genes in other pathways (Supplementary file 3K).
evidence: The manuscript reports control analysis to exclude potential artifacts.

claim: RNA half-life was positively associated with the RNA–protein correlation (rho = 0.51, p=0.001).
source: In addition, we also observed that RNA half-life was positively associated with the RNA–protein correlation (rho = 0.51, p=0.001)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical association between RNA half-life and RNA-protein correlation.

claim: RNA half-life was negatively associated with the DNA–RNA correlation (rho = −0.52, p=0.002).
source: and was negatively associated with the DNA–RNA correlation (rho = −0.52, p=0.002)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical association between RNA half-life and DNA-RNA correlation.

claim: No association was found between protein half-life and DNA-RNA or RNA-protein correlations.
source: while no such association was found for protein half-life (Supplementary file 3J, see 'Discussion').
evidence: The manuscript reports lack of association between protein half-life and correlations.

claim: A recent study showed that protein regulation in aneuploid cells is associated with protein regulation in normal cells.
source: A recent study showed that protein regulation in aneuploid cells is associated with protein regulation in normal cells (McShane et al., 2016)
